title: Governing Authorities, the Debt of Love, and the Coming Day
summary: Paul tells believers to submit to the governing authorities, since all authority comes from God, and rulers serve God by restraining wrongdoing, which is why believers pay taxes and give respect and honor where due. He then says the only debt they should carry is the continuing debt of love, because love fulfills the law. The chapter closes with a call to wake up, since the night is nearly over, and to put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
story: Chapter 12 ended with the refusal of revenge: believers must leave vengeance to God and overcome evil with good. Chapter 13 continues the thought by describing one of the ways God restrains evil in the present age, through governing authorities. It then returns to love, which was the heading of the commands in 12:9, and to the hope of the coming day that has run through the letter since chapter 8. These three topics belong together. Believers live under earthly rulers, but they owe their deepest debt to love, and they live in the light of a day that will outlast every earthly authority.
historical:
Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, early in the reign of the emperor Nero, who came to power in AD 54 at sixteen. His first years were remembered as relatively stable, when advisers such as the philosopher Seneca and the prefect Burrus had strong influence. The later cruelties of his reign, including the persecution of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64, were still in the future, and Christian tradition holds that Paul himself was executed in Rome under Nero. Jewish residents of Rome had been expelled under Claudius around AD 49, an experience that gave the church good reason to avoid needless conflict with the authorities. The Roman historian Tacitus reports public complaints about the conduct of tax collectors around AD 58, which suggests that taxes were a live issue in the city when the letter arrived.

Paul distinguishes two kinds of payment in verse 7. The first word (phoros) usually refers to direct taxes paid by subject peoples, and the second (telos) to indirect taxes such as tolls and customs duties. Jesus had addressed the same issue when he told his questioners to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God (Mark 12:17).
cultural:
In the Roman world, political authority was bound up with religion. Emperors were honored with temples and sacrifices in many cities, and loyalty to Rome was expressed through religious acts. Paul does something striking here: he says the authorities exist because God appointed them and calls them God's servants. That both grants them real authority and places them under a higher one. The Roman official did not rule by his own divinity but as a servant accountable to the God of Israel.

The "sword" in verse 4 was a symbol of a magistrate's power to punish, including capital punishment, which provincial governors held. The call to wake up at dawn draws on the ordinary rhythm of a city without electric light, where night was the time for drinking parties, sexual license, and street violence, and day the time for honest work. Paul's list in verse 13 describes exactly the kind of night life for which Roman cities were known.
literary: The chapter has three sections. Verses 1 to 7 are a compact argument: a command (submit), a reason (authority comes from God), consequences (resisting authority is resisting God), and practical application (pay taxes, give respect). The word "authority" or "authorities" repeats throughout, as do the words for fear and good and evil. Verses 8 to 10 turn on a wordplay: owe nothing to anyone except love, a debt that can never be fully paid. Paul summarizes several of the Ten Commandments under the command of Leviticus 19:18 to love one's neighbor as oneself. Verses 11 to 14 use the images of night and day, sleep and waking, and taking off and putting on clothes or armor, images Paul uses elsewhere as well (1 Thessalonians 5:4-8; Ephesians 6:11-17).

outline.t: The one continuing debt: love fulfills the law
The night is nearly over: put on Christ

doctrines.note: All authority comes from God, and even rulers who do not know him hold their office under his providence. This means earthly power is real but never ultimate, because rulers are called servants of God and are accountable to him.
Love fulfills the law. Paul does not abolish the commandments but shows their purpose: each one names a way of refusing to harm the neighbor, and love does no wrong to its neighbor.
Salvation is nearer now than when believers first believed. The coming day gives urgency and shape to present conduct, as believers live now in a way that fits the day to come.

words.note: Hupotasso, to submit, to place oneself under an order. It describes acknowledging one's place in an ordered relationship, and in the New Testament it is used of relations in households, churches, and states. It is not identical with unconditional obedience; the same apostles who taught submission refused to stop preaching when ordered to do so (Acts 4:19-20; 5:29).

Diakonos, servant or minister. Paul uses this word, which he also uses for himself and for Phoebe in 16:1, to describe the ruler as God's servant for the people's good. The title both honors and limits the ruler. A servant acts on behalf of a master and is answerable to him.

Anakephalaioomai, to sum up or gather under one head. Paul says the commandments are summed up in the command to love one's neighbor. The same word is used in Ephesians 1:10 for God's purpose to gather all things together in Christ.

Enduo, to put on or clothe oneself. It appears in verse 12 (the armor of light) and verse 14 (the Lord Jesus Christ). In Galatians 3:27 Paul says those baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ. The image suggests taking on his character and identity as one would put on clothes for the day.

christ: Christ appears at the chapter's climax: believers are to "clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ" (verse 14). The coming day is the day of his return, the salvation that is nearer than when they believed. Christ is also the key to reading the first section. He himself submitted to Roman authority to the point of death while insisting that Pilate would have no authority unless it had been given from above (John 19:11). His followers owe the governing authorities respect and taxes, but they confess Jesus as Lord (10:9), a title the Roman world was used to giving to Caesar. The command to love one's neighbor as oneself is the one Jesus named as the second greatest commandment (Mark 12:31).

hard.q: Does Romans 13 require Christians to obey every government, however unjust?
hard.a:
Paul's words are general and direct, and they have been read in several ways across Christian history. Paul was writing to a small community in the capital of an empire that did not yet persecute Christians as such, and he describes government as it ought to function: rewarding good and punishing evil. The passage does not address what believers should do when rulers command evil or punish good, though other Scripture does. The apostles told the council in Jerusalem that they must obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5:29), and Revelation 13 portrays imperial power turned against God's people as a beast.

Christian traditions have drawn different conclusions. Augustine distinguished the city of God from the earthly city, which believers use and respect but never worship. Martin Luther taught two kingdoms, in which God governs the world through the state and the church through the gospel, and he generally urged obedience to rulers. John Calvin also taught obedience but allowed that lesser magistrates might resist tyranny, an idea later Reformed writers developed further. Anabaptist traditions emphasize the church's separateness from the state and nonviolence. The passage has been used to urge compliance with unjust regimes, and it has also been read by Christians who resisted such regimes, such as those in the Confessing Church in Germany in the 1930s, who argued that a state claiming total authority had exceeded what God gives. Most Christian traditions agree that believers owe government real respect, obedience in lawful matters, and taxes, and that no government may claim the allegiance that belongs to God alone. They differ on when and how resistance is justified.

questions: Paul calls rulers God's servants. How does that both honor and limit those who hold power in your own setting?
What would it mean to treat love as a debt you never finish paying, rather than a favor you choose to give?
The chapter ends with a call to wake up because the day is near. What in your life belongs to the night, and what would it look like to put on Christ instead?
